questions.stem: Aggregate demand policies are used mainly to:
options: expand the economy's productive capacity over the long term
correct market failures, such as pollution, in individual markets across the economy
hold the exchange rate at a fixed level against the US dollar
stabilise the business cycle by smoothing fluctuations in spending
questions.explanation: Monetary and budgetary policy influence total spending, so they are used to dampen booms and soften downturns. Expanding productive capacity over the long term is the role of aggregate supply policies.

questions.stem: The economy is in a downturn, with rising cyclical unemployment and inflation below target. The appropriate monetary policy response is to:
options: keep the cash rate steady until inflation rises above the target band
raise the cash rate to support the value of the dollar
lower the cash rate to stimulate aggregate demand
raise the cash rate to reduce aggregate demand
questions.explanation: Weak demand and low inflation call for an expansionary stance, so the RBA would cut the cash rate to encourage borrowing and spending. Raising rates would deepen the downturn.

questions.stem: The main monetary policy goals of the Reserve Bank of Australia include:
options: high company profits and low wages growth
price stability and full employment
a balanced budget and low public debt
a fixed exchange rate and a current account surplus
questions.explanation: The RBA conducts monetary policy to keep inflation low and stable and to support full employment, for the welfare of Australians. Budget outcomes and public debt are matters for the government's budgetary policy.

questions.stem: The RBA's inflation target is for annual consumer price inflation to be:
options: between 0 and 1 per cent
between 3 and 5 per cent
below 1 per cent in every quarter
between 2 and 3 per cent
questions.explanation: The RBA aims to keep inflation within a target band of 2 to 3 per cent. A low, positive target avoids the costs of high inflation and the risks of deflation.

questions.stem: The RBA conducts monetary policy independently of the government. A key benefit of this independence is that:
options: decisions are less likely to be driven by short-term political pressures
the RBA can also set the government's tax rates and spending levels each year
changes in interest rates no longer affect the value of the dollar
monetary policy no longer needs to aim at a target for inflation
questions.explanation: An independent central bank can raise interest rates when needed, even if that is politically unpopular. That makes its commitment to low inflation more credible.

questions.stem: By keeping inflation within its target band over time, the RBA aims to:
options: keep the federal budget in surplus by raising tax revenue from interest income
eliminate structural unemployment by matching workers' skills to available jobs
anchor expectations, so wages and prices are set consistent with low inflation
ensure that the Australian dollar appreciates against other currencies each year
questions.explanation: If households and firms expect inflation to stay near target, they set wages and prices accordingly, which helps keep inflation there. Structural unemployment needs supply-side policies, not monetary policy.

questions.stem: The cash rate is:
options: the interest rate the government pays on ten-year bonds
the interest rate that banks pay on household savings accounts
the interest rate on overnight loans between financial institutions
the interest rate charged on standard variable home loans
questions.explanation: The cash rate is the rate at which banks lend funds to each other overnight. It is the RBA's operational target, and changes in it flow through to other interest rates.

questions.stem: Conventional monetary policy in Australia involves the RBA:
options: setting a target for the cash rate and using market operations to keep the actual rate near it
setting the interest rates that each commercial bank must charge on its home loans and business loans
changing personal income tax rates to raise or lower household disposable income
buying and selling Australian dollars to hold the exchange rate at a fixed level
questions.explanation: The RBA announces a cash rate target and manages the supply of funds in the money market so the actual cash rate stays close to it. It does not set the rates banks charge customers, and tax rates are set by the government.

questions.stem: A change in the cash rate target affects other interest rates in the economy mainly because:
options: the exchange rate adjusts and fixes every other interest rate at the same level
banks' funding costs change, and banks generally pass this on to lending and deposit rates
the RBA directly sets the interest rate on every mortgage, business loan and personal loan in Australia
the government passes a law requiring banks to match each change in the cash rate
questions.explanation: The cash rate influences what banks pay for their own funds, so banks adjust the rates they charge borrowers and pay depositors. The pass-through is a market response, not a legal requirement.

questions.stem: A cut in the cash rate may not be passed on in full to borrowers because:
options: borrowers must first agree in writing to each reduction in their interest rate
banks' other funding costs, such as deposit rates and overseas borrowing costs, may not fall as much
the RBA requires banks to keep their lending rates unchanged for at least a year after a cut in the cash rate
lending rates on home loans are set by the federal government in each budget
questions.explanation: Banks fund their lending from several sources, and only some costs move one for one with the cash rate. If other funding costs fall by less, banks may cut lending rates by less than the cash rate.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of an unconventional monetary policy tool?
options: An increase in the rate of personal income tax
A rise in payments to people receiving unemployment benefits
Large-scale purchases of government bonds (quantitative easing)
A 0.25 percentage point cut in the cash rate target
questions.explanation: Quantitative easing is unconventional because it works through the central bank's balance sheet rather than the cash rate target. Changes to taxes and benefits are budgetary policy.

questions.stem: Quantitative easing aims to stimulate aggregate demand mainly by:
options: buying bonds to lower longer-term interest rates and add liquidity to the financial system
selling bonds to raise longer-term interest rates and reduce the amount of lending by banks
raising the cash rate target from near zero to encourage saving
increasing government spending directly on goods and services
questions.explanation: When a central bank buys bonds in large amounts, bond prices rise and their yields fall, lowering long-term borrowing costs. The purchases also add funds to the banking system, supporting lending and spending.

questions.stem: Central banks typically turn to unconventional monetary policy tools when:
options: the cash rate is already close to zero and further stimulus is needed
inflation is well above target and the economy is booming
unemployment is below the NAIRU and wages are rising fast
the budget is in surplus and public debt is falling
questions.explanation: Once the cash rate is near its lower bound, there is little room to cut further, so central banks use other tools to lower borrowing costs. In a boom with high inflation, the response would be to raise the cash rate.

questions.stem: The RBA announces that it does not expect to raise the cash rate until inflation is sustainably within the target band. This unconventional tool is known as:
options: a term funding facility
forward guidance
quantitative easing
yield curve control
questions.explanation: Forward guidance is a statement about the likely future path of policy, intended to shape expectations and lower longer-term interest rates. Quantitative easing and yield targets involve buying bonds, and a term funding facility provides cheap loans to banks.

questions.stem: The transmission mechanism of monetary policy describes:
options: how changes in the cash rate flow through to spending, aggregate demand and inflation
how the federal government sets the RBA's cash rate target as part of each annual budget
how tax revenue is distributed between the states and territories
how the exchange rate is fixed by the Treasury each year
questions.explanation: The transmission mechanism traces how a cash rate change affects other interest rates, then spending decisions, then output, employment and inflation. The cash rate is set by the RBA, not in the budget.

questions.stem: Through the savings and investment channel, a cut in interest rates:
options: causes the dollar to appreciate, which reduces Australia's net exports
reduces the reward for saving and lowers the cost of borrowing to spend and invest
raises the return on saving, so households choose to spend less of their income
lowers the value of assets such as shares and housing, so household wealth falls
questions.explanation: Lower rates make saving less attractive and borrowing cheaper, so households consume more and firms invest more. Both raise aggregate demand.

questions.stem: Through the cash-flow channel, a rise in interest rates reduces spending because:
options: households with variable-rate mortgages have less disposable income after repayments
it raises the value of the wealth that households hold in housing, shares and superannuation
it lowers the exchange rate and makes imported goods dearer
it lowers the interest costs that firms pay on their business loans
questions.explanation: Higher repayments take a larger share of borrowers' incomes, leaving less for other spending. The cash-flow channel works through the income left over after interest payments.

questions.stem: Under the exchange rate channel, a cut in the cash rate relative to overseas interest rates tends to:
options: appreciate the dollar, raising net exports and aggregate demand
depreciate the dollar, lowering net exports and aggregate demand
appreciate the dollar, lowering import prices and inflation
depreciate the dollar, raising net exports and aggregate demand
questions.explanation: Lower relative interest rates reduce capital inflow, so the dollar tends to fall. A lower dollar makes exports cheaper and imports dearer, lifting net exports.

questions.stem: The asset prices and wealth channel works because lower interest rates tend to:
options: raise the prices of housing and shares, so households feel wealthier and spend more
reduce the price of housing as builders respond to cheaper finance by constructing more homes
lower household wealth, so households cut their spending to rebuild savings
raise the cost of borrowing to buy assets such as houses and shares
questions.explanation: Lower rates make assets more attractive and cheaper to finance, so their prices rise. Higher wealth encourages households to spend more, and higher housing prices also support new building.

questions.stem: After a cash rate rise, a retired couple living on interest from term deposits increase their spending. Which channel of the transmission mechanism does this reflect?
options: The exchange rate channel
The asset prices and wealth channel
The cash-flow channel
The savings and investment channel
questions.explanation: Higher rates raise interest income for savers, which increases their cash flow and spending, even though this works against the policy's aim. The savings and investment channel concerns the incentive to save rather than spend, which would reduce spending.

questions.stem: A rise in the cash rate can reduce inflation through the exchange rate channel because:
options: an appreciation increases overseas demand for Australian exports
a depreciation reduces Australian demand for imported goods
an appreciation lowers the Australian dollar price of imported goods
a depreciation raises the Australian dollar price of imported goods
questions.explanation: Higher relative interest rates tend to lift the dollar, which makes imports cheaper in Australian dollars and directly lowers prices in the CPI. An appreciation reduces, rather than increases, demand for exports.

questions.stem: An expansionary (accommodative) monetary policy stance involves:
options: setting the cash rate high to slow aggregate demand
increasing government spending on infrastructure
keeping the cash rate at its neutral level
setting the cash rate low to stimulate aggregate demand
questions.explanation: An expansionary stance means interest rates are low enough to encourage borrowing and spending. A high cash rate is contractionary, and government spending is budgetary policy.

questions.stem: A neutral monetary policy stance means the cash rate is set at a level that:
options: keeps the federal budget balanced each year
maximises the rate of economic growth each year
neither stimulates nor restrains aggregate demand
is equal to zero in nominal terms
questions.explanation: The neutral rate is the cash rate consistent with stable inflation and full employment, neither adding to nor subtracting from demand. A rate below neutral is expansionary and a rate above it is contractionary.

questions.stem: The RBA raises the cash rate target several times in a year as inflation rises above the target band. Its stance has become:
options: more expansionary, to boost aggregate demand
more contractionary, to raise aggregate demand
neutral, as the rate changes cancel out
more contractionary, to slow aggregate demand
questions.explanation: Raising the cash rate makes borrowing dearer and saving more rewarding, which slows spending and inflation. That is a move towards a contractionary, or restrictive, stance.

questions.stem: In a hypothetical economy, the cash rate is 3 per cent and inflation is 4 per cent. The real cash rate is about:
options: 7 per cent, suggesting a contractionary stance
−1 per cent, suggesting a contractionary stance
−1 per cent, suggesting an expansionary stance
1 per cent, suggesting a contractionary stance
questions.explanation: The real rate is approximately the nominal rate minus inflation: 3 − 4 = −1 per cent. A negative real cash rate is below any plausible neutral rate, so it encourages borrowing and spending.

questions.stem: Which situation calls for a contractionary monetary policy stance?
options: Inflation is below the target band and unemployment is rising
Real GDP is falling and consumer confidence is weak
Prices are falling and firms have large amounts of spare capacity
Inflation is above the target band and unemployment is below the NAIRU
questions.explanation: When demand is pushing inflation above target and the labour market is tight, the RBA raises the cash rate to slow spending. The other situations show weak demand, which calls for an expansionary stance.

questions.stem: Inflation is within the target band, unemployment is close to the NAIRU and growth is near trend. The RBA is most likely to:
options: keep the cash rate close to its neutral level
cut the cash rate sharply to boost growth
raise the cash rate sharply to cut inflation
begin large-scale purchases of government bonds
questions.explanation: When the goals are being met, there is no need to stimulate or restrain demand, so a neutral setting is appropriate. Large bond purchases are used when the cash rate is near zero and more stimulus is needed.

questions.stem: The main aim of a contractionary monetary policy is to:
options: increase aggregate supply by lowering firms' costs of production
weaken the dollar so that exporters become more competitive
slow the growth of aggregate demand and bring inflation back to target
raise aggregate demand and reduce cyclical unemployment in a downturn
questions.explanation: Higher interest rates reduce borrowing and spending, easing demand pressure on prices. A contractionary policy tends to strengthen rather than weaken the dollar.

questions.stem: A rise in the cash rate that brings inflation back to target is also likely to:
options: slow economic growth and raise unemployment in the short term
speed up economic growth and reduce unemployment in the short term
raise inflation in the long run by lowering firms' borrowing costs
raise the participation rate by making work more attractive
questions.explanation: Slower spending means less output and less demand for labour, so there is a short-term trade-off between the inflation goal and the growth and employment goals. Keeping inflation low supports these goals over the longer term.

questions.stem: Lower interest rates can raise material living standards mainly by:
options: raising the interest income received by savers
reducing environmental damage from production
boosting spending, output and employment
lowering the price of every good and service
questions.explanation: Cheaper borrowing lifts consumption and investment, which raises output and creates jobs, so more people have income to spend. Lower rates reduce, rather than raise, savers' interest income.

questions.stem: A strength of monetary policy is that it has a short implementation lag, because:
options: its full effects on spending and inflation appear within a month of a change
the government must legislate each change, which ensures broad support for it in parliament
banks are required by law to change their lending rates on the same day
the RBA can decide and announce a change in the cash rate without parliament's approval
questions.explanation: The RBA meets regularly and can change the cash rate at short notice, without legislation. The time it takes for the change to affect spending, the impact lag, is much longer.

questions.stem: The RBA's credibility is a strength of monetary policy because:
options: it allows the RBA to set any exchange rate it chooses for the Australian dollar each day
it removes the need for the government to use budgetary policy
it ensures every change in the cash rate takes effect immediately
if people trust it to keep inflation low, inflation expectations stay anchored
questions.explanation: When households and firms believe the RBA will act to keep inflation near target, they build low inflation into wage and price decisions. That makes inflation easier to control.

questions.stem: A weakness of monetary policy is that:
options: it raises the economy's productive capacity too quickly to control inflation
its effect on spending can take a year or more to come through in full
each change in the cash rate must first be approved by federal parliament
it can be aimed at a single industry or region without affecting others
questions.explanation: Monetary policy has a long and variable impact lag, so the RBA must act on forecasts of where the economy is heading. It does not need parliamentary approval.

questions.stem: Monetary policy is often described as a blunt instrument because:
options: a change in the cash rate affects all regions and sectors, whatever their conditions
the RBA is only permitted to change the cash rate once in each financial year, after the budget
a change in the cash rate affects only the housing market and no other sector
its effects on spending are always felt immediately and in full
questions.explanation: One cash rate applies across the whole economy, so a rate rise to cool a booming region also slows regions that are already weak. Budgetary policy can be targeted more precisely.

questions.stem: Cuts in the cash rate may have little effect on spending when:
options: inflation is above the target band and rising
the dollar is depreciating against other currencies
households and firms are pessimistic and reluctant to borrow
consumer confidence is high and borrowing is strong
questions.explanation: Cheaper credit only stimulates demand if people are willing to borrow and spend. When confidence is low, households may save and firms may delay investment despite low rates.

questions.stem: Monetary policy is less effective in dealing with inflation caused by a supply shock because:
options: raising rates to curb inflation further weakens output that the shock has already reduced
the RBA is only able to raise interest rates and is not permitted to cut them during a supply shock
cost inflation caused by supply shocks does not show up in the Consumer Price Index
supply shocks always disappear within a month, before any policy could take effect
questions.explanation: A supply shock raises prices and reduces output at the same time. Higher interest rates can slow inflation only by cutting demand further, which deepens the fall in output and employment.

questions.stem: A weakness of using higher interest rates to slow spending is that:
options: it has no effect on the value of the dollar or on Australia's exports
the burden falls heavily on households with large variable-rate mortgages
it raises the disposable incomes of all borrowers with variable-rate loans
it reduces the interest income received by retirees who hold term deposits
questions.explanation: Rate rises reduce spending largely by squeezing borrowers, so recent home buyers with big loans bear much of the cost. Savers with deposits actually gain interest income.

questions.stem: The RBA cuts the cash rate, but at the same time central banks overseas cut their rates by more. The exchange rate channel is likely to:
options: be strengthened, as Australian assets become less attractive
be weakened, as the Australian dollar may appreciate rather than fall
be strengthened, as the Australian dollar depreciates sharply
be unaffected, as only Australian interest rates influence the dollar
questions.explanation: What matters for capital flows is the gap between Australian and overseas rates. If overseas rates fall further, Australian rates rise in relative terms, so the dollar may rise, working against the stimulus.
